cues.text: A Hard Childhood
Born at Ravenna in 1007, the youngest child of a large, impoverished noble family, Peter was so unwanted at birth that his own mother initially refused to nurse him.
After his parents' deaths, one brother forced him to work as a swineherd.
Another brother, an archpriest named Damian, took him in and gave him a genuine education.
Peter later adopted his benefactor's name in gratitude, becoming 'Peter Damian.'
From Teacher to Hermit
A gifted student at Faenza and Parma, Peter became a respected teacher before abandoning a promising academic career around 1035 to enter the austere hermitage of Fonte Avellana in the Apennines.

By 1043 he had been elected prior, reorganizing the community's life by combining the ideals of St. Benedict and St. Romuald, and going on to found five additional hermitages under similar reformed observance.
Voice of Church Reform

From his hermitage, Peter Damian became one of the sharpest and most influential voices calling for reform of an eleventh-century Church badly troubled by simony (the buying and selling of church offices) and clerical unchastity.

His treatise Liber Gomorrhianus attacked moral corruption among the clergy with blunt severity, while his Liber Gratissimus defended the validity of orders even when conferred by simonist bishops, a nuanced position amid the reform movement's fiercer voices.
Reluctant Cardinal
Pope Stephen IX elevated Peter to Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia in 1057 against his own strong preference to remain a simple hermit.
In this office he served as a trusted papal legate on sensitive missions across Italy, France, and Germany.
Once, he persuaded a German king not to divorce his wife and helped settle disputes between rival claimants to sees and even between antipopes contesting Rome itself.
A Champion of Papal Elections
Peter Damian played a role in the landmark Lateran Synod of 1059.

It established a new procedure in which the cardinal bishops would lead the election, with the other cardinals and the Roman clergy participating, while retaining a role for the Roman people and acknowledging the emperor's confirmation privilege.
This reform helped limit the interference of secular rulers in papal elections.
Legacy

Granted permission late in life to return to his beloved hermitage, Peter Damian nonetheless continued to serve the Holy See when called upon, dying at Faenza in 1072 while returning from a reconciliation mission to Ravenna.
Never formally canonized in the medieval sense, his cultus flourished spontaneously after death.
Pope Leo XII extended his feast to the universal Church and declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1828.
This honored a monk-reformer whose fierce writings and personal example did much to prepare the ground for the broader Gregorian Reform of the following decades.
